title: What are varargs and what are the rules for using them?
shortTitle: What are varargs and what are the rules?
keyPoints: Varargs (String... args) lets a method accept zero or more arguments of the same type
The compiler converts varargs to an array internally – the method receives a regular array
Varargs must be the LAST parameter: process(String id, BigDecimal... amounts) is OK
Only ONE varargs parameter per method – two varargs parameters do not compile
Varargs creates a new array on every call – avoid in hot paths for performance
Varargs can cause ambiguity with overloaded methods – the compiler picks the most specific match

s1_definition.oneliner: Varargs (type... name) lets a method accept zero or more arguments of the same type. The compiler creates an array behind the scenes.
s1_definition.profdef:
Varargs is syntactic sugar for arrays:

- **Syntax:** `public void process(BigDecimal... amounts)` accepts zero or more BigDecimal arguments.
- **Internally:** The compiler converts it to `process(BigDecimal[] amounts)`. The bytecode is identical.
- **Calling:** You can pass individual values: `process(a, b, c)` or an array: `process(new BigDecimal[]{a, b, c})` or nothing: `process()`.
- **Rules:** Must be last parameter. Only one per method.
s1_definition.analogy: A bank deposit slip with a variable number of amount fields. You can write one amount, five amounts, or no amounts at all. The teller processes whatever you provide, treating them all as a list internally.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Source:  process(BigDecimal... amounts)
  Bytecode: process(BigDecimal[] amounts)
  → identical at runtime

  Calling:
    process(a, b, c)           → compiler creates new BigDecimal[]{a, b, c}
    process()                  → compiler creates new BigDecimal[]{}
    process(existingArray)     → uses the array directly

  Rules:
    must be LAST parameter
    only ONE per method
    zero arguments allowed
    exact match wins over varargs in overloading
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Varargs lets a method accept zero or more arguments of the same type using the `type... name` syntax. The compiler converts it to an array internally, so the method receives a regular array. You can call it with individual values, with an array, or with no arguments at all.

The rules are simple: varargs must be the last parameter, and only one varargs parameter is allowed per method. In overloading, an exact match beats a varargs match. Two competing varargs overloads can cause ambiguity.

In banking, varargs is useful for methods that accept a variable number of amounts, IDs, or flags. But for hot paths, pass a pre-built array to avoid the allocation overhead of creating a new array on every call.

One sentence to remember: varargs (type... name) is syntactic sugar for an array parameter – must be last, only one per method, and creates a new array on each call.
